name: Tech neck correction

lead: Tech neck, or text neck, is a forward-leaning head posture linked to long hours on phones and laptops. Correcting it is used to bring the head back over the shoulders, which looksmaxxers say lengthens the visual neck line and cleans up the jaw-to-neck transition in profile.

Approaches described in clinical sources strengthen the deep neck flexors and scapular muscles, stretch tight posterior neck muscles and cut sustained screen-flexed positions. A 2023 scoping review found no agreed definition of text neck; published work covers pain, posture measurement and neck skin changes rather than facial or jaw appearance.

paras: People combine posture awareness, breaks from screens, raising screen height, and strengthening and stretching of the neck and upper back. It is usually built into daily habits and a few exercise sessions a week, with posture changes building over weeks to months.
Posture exercises are generally described as low risk. People with neck pain or neurological symptoms are usually advised by clinicians to get assessed first.

web.title: Keep your head up: 'Text neck' takes a toll on the spine
Forward head posture and neck pain meta-analysis

angle.text: Undoing forward head posture from screen use brings the head back over the shoulders, which is said to lengthen the visible neck and give a cleaner jaw-to-neck transition. Exercises and ergonomic habits are studied for neck pain and posture.

lead: Tech neck, also called text neck, is an informal name for a forward-leaning head and neck posture associated with prolonged use of phones, tablets and laptops, and for the discomfort sometimes attributed to it. "Tech neck correction" refers to the exercises, ergonomic changes and posture habits that people use to bring the head back over the shoulders. In looksmaxxing culture it is discussed as a posture topic: proponents say an upright head position lengthens the visible neck line, sharpens the jaw-to-neck transition and reduces the look of a forward-poking chin, and that it also makes a person appear taller and more confident.[1][2]

Clinically, the pattern is called forward head posture, with the ear sitting ahead of the shoulder; combined with rounded shoulders it is called upper crossed syndrome.[1] A 2023 scoping review of 41 articles found that text neck is defined inconsistently, most often by posture (in 92.7 percent of articles), overuse, mechanical stress and musculoskeletal symptoms.[3]

Correction approaches described in the physiotherapy literature include strengthening the deep neck flexors and the muscles that retract the shoulder blades, stretching the upper trapezius, mobilising the upper back, taking breaks from screens and adjusting screen height.[1][4] Research to date measures pain, disability and posture angles; no published study has tested whether correcting tech neck changes jawline or facial appearance. Popular coverage of the topic, such as a 2014 report on a spine-surgeon's load analysis, has focused on how much force a forward-tilted head places on the neck.[5]

paras: Wikipedia describes forward head posture as the head sitting ahead of the shoulders, commonly measured by the position of the ear relative to the shoulder, with the chin poked forward and in some cases the upper back more rounded; it links most cases to hours of hunching over laptops, tablets and phones. Occupations such as dentistry, surgery, hairdressing and desk work are also listed.[1] When combined with rounded shoulders the pattern is called upper crossed syndrome.[1]

"Tech neck" and "text neck" are popular terms rather than formal diagnoses. The 2023 scoping review searched five databases and found 41 articles using the terms; definitions varied, with overuse in 63.4 percent, mechanical stress in 41.4 percent and musculoskeletal symptoms in 36.6 percent.[3]

Wikipedia's account of the mechanics says that tilting the head forward increases the load carried by the neck muscles and joints because of the longer lever arm, that the deep neck flexors are used little in this position, and that the back-of-neck muscles shorten with sustained strain.[1] The page flags several of these statements as needing further confirmation.[1]

Wikipedia lists the signs of forward head posture as an ear lobe sitting ahead of a vertical line through the shoulder's acromion and a chin that pokes forward; symptoms it names include overuse pain and fatigue along the back of the neck and mid-back, often starting in the upper trapezius, and cervicogenic headache.[1] The page also flags several statements, including parts of its account of mechanism and treatment, as needing better sourcing.[1]

A frequently cited analysis by spine surgeon Kenneth Hansraj, published in Surgical Technology International in 2014, modelled the force on the cervical spine at different degrees of forward head tilt. As reported by public radio, an adult head weighs about 10 to 12 pounds in the neutral position, and the modelled load rose to about 27 pounds at 15 degrees of tilt and about 60 pounds at 60 degrees.[5] Hansraj's paper argues that people spend an estimated 700 to 1,400 hours a year with the head tilted forward and that these stresses may contribute to early wear and degeneration; he advises looking at phones by lowering the eyes instead of the head and keeping the ears aligned over the shoulders with the shoulder blades drawn back.[5]

The figures come from a model rather than from a measurement of people, and were widely repeated in news coverage. Wikipedia's forward head posture page repeats a rule of roughly 10 pounds of added load per inch of forward head position, citing the same paper.[1]

The 2023 scoping review notes that definitions of text neck are not standardised: 92.7 percent of the 41 articles defined it through posture, 63.4 percent through overuse, 41.4 percent through mechanical stress and 36.6 percent through musculoskeletal symptoms.[3] Clinical forward head posture is described by the ear-over-shoulder relationship.[1] Trials of correction exercises commonly report the craniovertebral angle, the angle between the neck and a horizontal line through the seventh cervical vertebra, together with neck disability scores.[6]

The sources link the posture to device use: Wikipedia notes that small portable devices cannot be set up ergonomically the way a desktop monitor can, so users hunch for many hours.[1] A 2012 Finnish study of school-age adolescents cited there associated more than two hours a day on computers with moderate or severe musculoskeletal pain.[1] The same article cites a 2019 meta-analysis that found a correlation between forward head posture and neck pain in adults but not in adolescents.[1] A 2026 review in the European Spine Journal describes the posture as a widespread, device-related spinal problem.[7]

A 2025 scoping review applied Hill's criteria of causation to 21 articles on text neck and neck pain, 90 percent of them observational, with a mean participant age around 24, and found that none of the criteria were met by any article; the authors concluded that a causal link was not supported by the current literature.[8] A 2022 review and a 2021 observational study in Spine also address the association between text neck and neck pain and mood.[9][10]

A 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis in Current Reviews in Musculoskeletal Medicine examined the relationship between forward head posture and neck pain.[11] Wikipedia reports its finding as a correlation in adults but not in adolescents.[1] A 2021 case-report paper in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health addressed text neck syndrome in children and adolescents,[12] and a 2026 Cureus narrative review illustrated ligament ossification with a case of a 61-year-old with heavy daily phone use, forward head posture and loss of cervical lordosis.[13] A 2026 paper in the Journal of the World Federation of Orthodontists is titled as examining the orthodontic implications of screen-time overload and tech neck.[14]

Sources on forward head posture describe strengthening of the deep neck flexors and scapular retractors, stretching of the upper trapezius, thoracic mobilization, regular breaks and ergonomic set-up as the usual approaches, and say a combination is likely to give lasting results.[1] A 2025 scoping review in the Journal of Clinical Medicine surveyed the physiotherapy methods used for text neck and noted that there is no consensus on rehabilitation.[15] A 2025 systematic review of systematic reviews of physiotherapy for upper cross syndrome concluded it is hard to separate each element of the syndrome and say which manual approach works best.[16]

Techniques tested in small trials include proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation (38 participants randomised to experimental or comparison groups),[17] and ELDOA stretching with post-facilitation stretching in adolescent smartphone users with text neck.[18] A 2024 study examined instrument-assisted soft tissue mobilization on specific muscles in people with tech neck.[19]

Further randomized trials in text neck syndrome have compared neck stabilisation plus Contrology (a Pilates-derived method) with conventional therapy,[20] and Global Postural Re-Education against comparison treatment.[21] Across these studies the outcomes are pain, disability and posture angles.

A 2025 pilot questionnaire study in a work setting examined how ergonomic tools, break frequency and posture awareness related to symptom intensity.[22] Wikipedia lists regular breaks while using mobile devices, posture awareness and ergonomic tools alongside strengthening and stretching.[1]

People who work on head position describe a similar set of habits: raising the phone or screen toward eye level, lowering the eyes rather than the head, taking breaks from screens, strengthening the muscles that pull the head back and the shoulder blades together, and stretching the muscles at the back of the neck and chest. Hansraj's own advice, as reported by the press, emphasises a neutral spine with ears aligned over the shoulders.[5] These are the physiotherapy and ergonomic approaches cited in the clinical sources above.[1][15]

A 2023 open-label study in Chinese women used a topical cosmeceutical regimen aimed at "tech neck" lines, meaning skin creasing on the neck in younger people, a different use of the term from posture.[23] The study was single-centre and had no control group. Its introduction lists neck and jawline ageing signs such as wrinkling, laxity, loss of mandibular contour, submental fat and platysma bands.[23]

Studies to date mostly concern symptoms and posture rather than appearance. The 2023 scoping review addressed definitions only.[3] A 2025 cross-sectional pilot questionnaire explored symptoms and preventive measures.[22] A 2024 trial-style study examined soft tissue mobilization.[19] Randomized trials in text neck syndrome have tested proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation,[17] ELDOA with post-facilitation stretching,[18] scapular retraction exercises versus the McKenzie method in university students with forward head posture (measuring craniovertebral angle and neck disability),[6] and Global Postural Re-Education.[21] A 2019 meta-analysis found a correlation between forward head posture and neck pain in adults but not adolescents.[11][1] No published study has tested whether correcting tech neck changes jawline or facial appearance.

Posture is treated in these communities as part of overall presentation: proponents say upright head carriage makes the neck look longer and the jaw more defined, and that devices and desk habits are a common cause of a forward head. The idea is that the jaw-to-neck angle and the visible length of the neck are partly a matter of where the head sits, so a head drawn back over the shoulders changes how a profile photo reads, the same way standing taller changes a full-body photo.

Head and neck posture is also discussed alongside tongue posture and jaw-related practices, and specific exercises associated with this goal, such as chin tucks, are covered in a separate article. Most discussion rests on before-and-after photos rather than measurement, and published studies of correction measure pain, disability and posture angles rather than facial appearance.

lore.intro: Tech neck correction is discussed in posture and looks communities as a way to improve neck length, jaw definition and general presence; most of the discussion rests on visual before-and-after impressions rather than measurement.

claims.claim: Forward head posture makes the jaw look weaker and the neck shorter.
Phones and laptops are the main cause of forward head posture.
Strengthening and stretching exercises can reverse the posture.
Correcting head posture visibly sharpens the jaw-to-neck line.
A forward-tilted head multiplies the load on the neck several times over.
Chin tucks and upper-back exercises fix tech neck.

timeline.event: Fejer and colleagues report adult neck pain point prevalence in the range of 5.9 to 22.2 percent, a figure cited on Wikipedia's forward head posture page.[1]
The iPhone is introduced; Wikipedia's account of forward head posture lists smartphones and tablets among the devices linked to sustained head-down posture.[1]
Hansraj publishes a widely cited analysis of cervical spine loading at different head-flexion angles; it is covered by MPR News in November.[1][5]
A systematic review and meta-analysis reports a correlation between forward head posture and neck pain in adults but not in adolescents.[11][1]
A study in Spine examines the association between text neck and neck pain in adults; a paper reviews text neck syndrome in children and adolescents.[10][12]
Scoping review of 41 articles finds no consensus definition of text neck; a randomized trial tests ELDOA with post-facilitation stretching.[3][18]
A randomized controlled trial tests proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation in text neck syndrome (38 participants).[17]
A scoping review applying Hill's criteria finds no causal link between text neck and neck pain established in the literature; a scoping review surveys physiotherapy for text neck.[8][15]
Randomized trials of scapular retraction versus McKenzie exercises and of Global Postural Re-Education are published.[6][21]
